newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany's Transrapid changes, stays on track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany's Transrapid changes, stays on track.

text.p: Germany's Transrapid rail consortium was restructured on Friday to keep the controversial magnetic-levitation project on track, although it now expects lower revenues and higher costs than previously forecast.

Three building groups quit the Transrapid consortium, leaving three industrial partners. National railway Deutsche Bahn AG will play a central role in the project, Transportation Minister Matthias Wissmann told a news conference.
"We will continue our work to realise the Transrapid with commitment and optimism," Wissmann said.
Wissmann said a new study showed the planned Hamburg-Berlin line would cost 10 percent more than the original nine-billion mark ($5.2 billion) projection.
Annual revenue is now seen at 790 million marks by 2010 in current prices -- down from an estimated 1.15 billion marks. Passenger traffic is also seen lower than initial estimates.

Dieter Vogel, chairman of Thyssen AG, the leading industrial partner in the project, said, "It is clear to all participants that the capital invested in the Hamburg-Berlin route will not earn an adequate return. But the project will still support itself under the lower traffic projections."

The Transrapid, whose trains glide on a magnetic cushion at speeds up to 420 kilometers per hour, is under attack by opposition parties and environmental groups who doubt there is sufficient demand for it in Germany.
Construction firms Phillip Holzmann, Hochtief and Bilfinger + Berger withdrew from the project under pressure from other partners to reduce costs, a Holzmann spokesman told Reuters.

Wissmann said the project would create 18,000 construction jobs and a further 4,400 to operate the system, and that construction of the Hamburg-Berlin line would now be opened for international bidding.
"Without a real tender, without real bidding, you don't get the competition you need, you don't get the cost reductions you need," Wissman told Reuters.

Existing partners Thyssen, Siemens AG and ADtranz -- a venture between car maker Daimler-Benz AG and Swiss-Swedish group ABB -- were negotiating with potential foreign investors and wanted to add another European partner, Wissmann said.
Siemens chairman Heinrich von Pierer said the group was talking to Anglo-French group GEC-Alsthom, makers of France's TGV high-speed trains.

Under current planning, construction is due to start in 1998, and operations begin in 2005. The government will cover the costs of the Hamburg-Berlin track, now seen at 6.1 billion marks, while the private-sector partners develop and operate the train. That cost is now estimated at 3.7 billion marks.

Industry officials say the Transrapid will help Germany keep a technological lead in high-speed rail. Despite domestic opposition, they hope the Hamburg-Berlin route will help them to sell the advanced technology in other countries.
"The baker can only sell his rolls if he is willing to eat them himself," von Pierer said.
Under the new structure, the private partners will put up 500 million marks in capital to form a financing company that will borrow 4.5 billion marks to cover start-up costs.

The Deutsche Bahn will pay a guaranteed annual sum -- set by a sliding scale based on revenue projections -- to the financing company for the use of the train. These fees will total 8.9 billion marks between 2005 and 2022.
Any revenue above 72 percent of the projected income will be divided by three and distributed among the private partners, the Deutsche Bahn and the federal government.

Opposition parties and environmentalist groups have vigorously attacked the project mainly on financial grounds, saying the the costs have been underestimated, demand overestimated, and that taxpayers will ultimately be forced to pick up the tab.
Thyssen's Vogel said, "The politics (of this project) have driven us nearly to the limit of what we can defend to our shareholders.... But the Transrapid has withstood this test."
($ = 1.714 German Marks)
